title: Your Phone's GPS Would Be Off by Miles Without Einstein
fb_caption:
Decoded: the blue dot on your map.
GPS satellite clocks run about 38 millionths of a second fast every day. Without Einstein's math, your position would drift by miles.
Did you know your phone only listens?
engagement_comment: 'Knew it' or 'no way': your phone never sends anything UP to GPS satellites. It only listens. 🛰️
sources: GPS satellites fly at about 20,200 km (12,550 miles); each circles the Earth twice a day; 24-slot constellation (31 operational as of mid-2023) keeps at least four in view: https://archive.gps.gov/systems/gps/space/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System

Satellites constantly broadcast signals; the receiver in your phone listens; a fix needs four or more satellites; GPS does not require the user to transmit any data: https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/gps/en/ ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System ; https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast162/Unit5/gps.html
Each satellite carries an atomic clock; signal travel time gives distance: https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast162/Unit5/gps.html ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Positioning_System

Relativity: motion slows the satellite clocks about 7 microseconds/day, weaker gravity speeds them up about 45, net about +38 microseconds/day: https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast162/Unit5/gps.html ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_analysis_for_the_Global_Positioning_System

Uncorrected, position errors would accumulate at about 10 km (6 miles) per day (one source: roughly 11.4 km/day); the clock rate is offset to compensate: https://www.astronomy.ohio-state.edu/pogge.1/Ast162/Unit5/gps.html ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_analysis_for_the_Global_Positioning_System

beats.text: The blue dot on your map knows which street you're on. Without Albert Einstein, it would be off by miles before the day was over. To see why, we have to go up. Way up.
Stop one: about 12,550 miles above you. More than two dozen GPS satellites are up here, and each one circles the entire Earth twice a day.
Stop two: one satellite, up close. It carries an atomic clock, and it broadcasts the same simple message over and over: here's who I am, and here's exactly what time it is.
Stop three: follow one of those signals back down to your hand. Notice the direction. The signals only come down. Your phone never sends anything up to those satellites. It just listens.

Stop four: a chip inside. It measures how long each signal took to arrive. Like counting the seconds between lightning and thunder, time becomes distance. With at least four satellites, it can work out where you are.

Here's the twist. Those clocks don't tick like clocks on the ground. The satellites move fast, which slows them a little. But gravity is weaker up there, which speeds them up more. Net result: they gain about 38 millionths of a second a day. Left uncorrected, your position would drift about six miles every day. So the fix is built in.

items: ABOUT 6 MILES OF DRIFT A DAY

beats.text: So every time that blue dot lands on the right street, Einstein gets proven right again. Another one decoded. Did you know your phone only listens? Comment knew it, or no way, and share this with whoever gets lost with the map open. Now look at that blue dot again.
